description: We are interested in technology, programming, and innovation. We enjoy learning new skills, exploring ideas, and solving problems together!
summary: LUNEX answers one question for the Moon's south pole: is it the right place and time to land? Pick a landing site and a date, and it shows the Sun and Earth against the real terrain horizon, hours of sunlight, solar power, when Earth is in view for direct radio, and the time left before sunset and Earthset, with a pass or fail and a calendar comparing every nearby date and site. It runs on NASA LRO LOLA terrain in the browser, agrees with NASA JPL Horizons to 0.0069 degrees, and serves the challenge's three audiences through three doors: mission planners, educators (Learn) and the public (Explore the Moon in 3D).
details:
What it does: At the Moon's south pole the Sun never climbs more than about 1.5 degrees above the horizon at the pole itself, so one ridge can switch power off for days and one rise can hide Earth, and with it direct radio, for a week. LUNEX lets anyone check a landing site and date in three choices: a place, an arrival date and a set of limits. It answers with a pass or fail, the stay hour by hour, the time left before sunset and Earthset, solar energy, and a calendar of twelve sites against arrival dates, so a slipped launch is re-checked in seconds.

How it works: Sun and Earth directions come from a Meeus and ELP-2000 engine in the Moon's Mean-Earth frame, checked against 1,338 JPL Horizons samples (worst error 0.0069 degrees). Terrain is nested NASA LRO LOLA data from 5 m to 480 m, horizons are marched to 400 km, and real shadows are cast in the browser. Results were validated against NASA's illumination maps (median difference 0.2 points), published sunlight studies (Connecting Ridge 78.1% against 78.1%) and NASA's permanently shadowed regions.

Three experiences, one engine: Mission Planners (landing check, workspace, scenario lab with delay, window finder, relocation and landing ellipse, reports), Learn (ten lessons that adapt from age 8 to university, simulations, challenges, a free educator pack, a different world for each audience), and Explore the Moon (fly to the pole, land at NASA's nine candidate regions in 3D with NASA's 1 m LRO and ShadowCam imagery, ask Nex, the guide).

Tools: TypeScript, Next.js, React, three.js, Web Workers, Vitest and Playwright. Code: https://github.com/Smart1po/lunex. Demo slides: https://lunar-landing-site-navigator.vercel.app/slides
